mainTopic: The greatness of rain, and how Torah stays with a worthy, humble person who learns together with others
overview: This amud first finishes the earlier discussion of the blessing on rain: we say both endings. Then it praises rain. רבי אבהו says rain is greater than תחיית המתים, while רב יוסף holds the two are equal. רב יהודה says the day of rain is as great as מתן תורה, and רבא says it is even greater. Both learn this from 'יערף כמטר לקחי'. From that same פסוק, רבא and רבי בנאה teach that Torah gives life to a worthy person who learns לשמה, but harms an unworthy one. A string of teachings follows about how to learn Torah. A worthy תלמיד חכם is like a fruit tree. Learning with others sharpens you, like iron on iron or sticks lighting a fire, and learning alone leads to foolishness. Teachers should seek out and teach worthy students. Torah stays only with a humble person, like water that flows down and wine that keeps in plain jars. The amud ends with the story of רבי יהושע בן חנניה and the emperor's daughter. At the end the emperor raises an objection, which is answered on the next amud.

steps.title: Say both endings of the thanksgiving blessing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes the earlier discussion: when thanking for rain, we say both 'אל ההודאות' and 'רוב ההודאות'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say both of them: 'God of thanksgivings' and 'Abundant thanksgivings.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line wraps up the discussion from just before this section about how to end the blessing said on rain. Two versions were suggested, and the ruling is to say both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, two different endings were offered for the blessing of thanks over rain. Instead of choosing one, the גמרא combines them so that nothing is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: God of thanksgivings, one ending of the blessing

steps.whatToRemember: When two good versions of a blessing exist, the גמרא here rules to say both.

phrases.english: Let us say both of them:
phrases.notes: This finishes a discussion from the previous page about how to end the blessing said on rain.

phrases.english: "God of thanksgivings" and "Abundant thanksgivings."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion from the previous page about the wording of the blessing on rain.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both endings, אל ההודאות and רוב ההודאות, are said together.

steps.title: Rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says the day of rain is greater than תחיית המתים, because rain helps everyone and not only the righteous.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: The day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead. Resurrection is only for the righteous, but rain is for both the righteous and the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins: praises of rain. רבי אבהו says rain is even greater than תחיית המתים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His measure of greatness is how many people benefit. תחיית המתים is a reward only for צדיקים, while rain falls for everyone, צדיקים and רשעים alike.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
The day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead,
for while the resurrection of the dead is for the righteous,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ גְּשָׁמִים — בֵּין לַצַּדִּיקִים בֵּין לָרְשָׁעִים.
phrases.english: rain is for both the righteous and the wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים מִתְּחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new series of statements praising rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is greater than תחיית המתים because it benefits both צדיקים and רשעים.

steps.title: רב יוסף holds rain and resurrection are equal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי אבהו argues with רב יוסף, who says rain is equal to תחיית המתים, which is why it is mentioned in that blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רב יוסף. רב יוסף said: Because rain is equal to the resurrection of the dead, the Sages placed its mention in the blessing of the resurrection of the dead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבי אבהו's statement does not fit with רב יוסף. רב יוסף holds that rain is only equal to תחיית המתים, not greater.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף explains why 'משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם' is said in the blessing of מחיה המתים in the שמונה עשרה: the two are equal. Calling them 'equal' does not fit with רבי אבהו's view that rain is greater, so the two opinions argue.

keyTerms.meaning: They set it in place, fixed it

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions agree that rain is very great. The argument is only whether rain is greater than תחיית המתים (רבי אבהו) or equal to it (רב יוסף).
steps.whyThisMatters: רב יוסף's statement explains why we mention rain in the second blessing of the שמונה עשרה, the blessing of מחיה המתים.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rav Yosef,
for Rav Yosef said:
Since it is equal to the resurrection of the dead,
they placed it in the blessing of the resurrection of the dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows an opinion that argues with רבי אבהו from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב יוסף, rain is equal to תחיית המתים, so its mention was placed in that blessing.

steps.title: The day of rain is as great as the giving of the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה compares the day of rain to the day of מתן תורה, learning it from a פסוק that compares Torah ('לקח') to rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: The day of rain is as great as the day the Torah was given, as it says: 'My lekach shall drop as the rain.' And 'lekach' means only Torah, as it says: 'For I have given you good lekach; do not forsake My Torah.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives another praise of rain: it is as great as the day the תורה was given. He proves it from two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק compares 'לקחי' to rain. The second פסוק shows that 'לקח' means Torah. Together they show that Torah is compared to rain, so the two are equal in greatness.

keyTerms.meaning: The day the Torah was given
Teaching, doctrine; here it means Torah
As it is said, introducing a פסוק

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:

phrases.aramaic: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים כְּיוֹם שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה בּוֹ תּוֹרָה,
phrases.english: The day of rain is as great as the day on which the Torah was given,
as it is said: "My teaching shall drop as the rain,"
and "lekach" means nothing other than Torah,
as it is said: "For I have given you good teaching;
do not forsake My Torah."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים כְּיוֹם שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה בּוֹ תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another praise of rain, this time comparing it to מתן תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The day of rain is as great as the day of מתן תורה, because the פסוק compares Torah to rain.

steps.title: רבא: Rain is even greater than the giving of the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבא says rain is greater than the day of מתן תורה, because in a comparison the smaller thing is compared to the bigger one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is greater than the day the Torah was given, as it says: 'My teaching shall drop as the rain.' Who is compared to whom? You must say the smaller is compared to the greater.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא uses the same פסוק as רב יהודה but goes further. He says rain is greater than מתן תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא uses a rule of comparisons: you describe the lesser thing by comparing it to the greater thing. Since the פסוק describes Torah 'like rain', rain must be the greater one.

keyTerms.meaning: Is hung on, compared to, depends on
You must say, the answer must be

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה: rain is equal to מתן תורה. רבא: rain is greater, because the smaller thing is compared to the greater one.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is greater than the day on which the Torah was given,
as it is said: "My teaching shall drop as the rain,"
Which one is compared to which?
You must say: the lesser is compared to the greater.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: יוֹתֵר מִיּוֹם שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה בּוֹ תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב יהודה's פסוק but draws a stronger conclusion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is greater than מתן תורה, since Torah is the one compared to rain.

steps.title: Is Torah like rain or like dew?
steps.stepSummary: רבא points out that the same פסוק compares Torah to strong rain and also to gentle dew.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised a contradiction: It is written 'My teaching shall drop as the rain,' and it is written 'My word shall flow as the dew'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא notices two images that seem to clash in the same פסוק. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'יערף כמטר' sounds forceful, like pounding rain. 'תזל כטל' sounds soft, like quiet dew. So which is it: is Torah harsh or gentle?

keyTerms.meaning: Raised a contradiction, threw two sources against each other

phrases.english: Rava raised a contradiction:
It is written: "My teaching shall drop as the rain,"
and it is written: "My word shall flow as the dew"!
phrases.notes: This is the next part of the same פסוק, דברים 32:2.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the same פסוק to look at a new question about it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two images in דברים 32:2, rain and dew
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rain is forceful and dew is gentle, so how can Torah be compared to both?

steps.title: Gentle for the worthy, harsh for the unworthy
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers: for a worthy תלמיד חכם Torah is gentle like dew. For an unworthy one it 'breaks his neck' like pounding rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy Torah scholar, it is like dew. If not, it breaks his neck like rain.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא resolves the contradiction. The two images describe two different kinds of people who learn Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a worthy scholar, Torah comes gently and helps him grow, like dew. For an unworthy one it becomes harmful. רבא reads 'יערף' as related to 'עורף', the back of the neck, so it 'breaks his neck' like heavy rain.

keyTerms.meaning: Breaks his neck (from עֹרֶף, back of the neck)

steps.whatToRemember: The same Torah is gentle like dew for a worthy scholar and harsh like rain for an unworthy one.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הָגוּן הוּא — כַּטַּל,
phrases.english: If he is a worthy Torah scholar, it is like dew,
and if not, it breaks his neck like the rain.
phrases.notes: A play on words: 'יערף' in the פסוק sounds like 'עורף', the back of the neck.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's contradiction from step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each image describes a different kind of person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seems to give two clashing descriptions of the same Torah.
steps.terutzMaskana: Dew describes Torah for a worthy scholar, and rain describes Torah for an unworthy one.

steps.title: Torah learned for its own sake is a medicine of life
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי בנאה: anyone who learns Torah לשמה finds that his Torah becomes a סם חיים. He proves it from three פסוקים in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי בנאה used to say: Whoever learns Torah for its own sake, his Torah becomes a medicine of life for him. As it says: 'It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it.' And it says: 'It shall be healing to your navel.' And it says: 'For whoever finds Me finds life.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports רבא's idea that Torah can affect two kinds of learners in opposite ways. This first half covers the good side: learning לשמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said Torah is gentle for a worthy scholar and harsh for an unworthy one. רבי בנאה gives the same split in clearer terms: what decides it is whether a person learns לשמה. Three פסוקים show that Torah brings life and healing to such a person.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the משנה)
For its own sake, with pure intentions
One who is busy with Torah study

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Bena'a would say:
Anyone who engages in Torah for its own sake —
his Torah becomes for him a medicine of life,
as it says: "It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it,"
and it says: "It shall be healing to your navel,"
and it says: "For whoever finds Me finds life."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's distinction in Step 7 with a ברייתא that splits learners into two groups.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's idea that Torah affects worthy and unworthy learners in opposite ways
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי בנאה and three פסוקים from משלי

steps.title: Torah learned not for its own sake is a poison of death
steps.stepSummary: רבי בנאה continues: Torah learned שלא לשמה becomes a סם המות. He reads the word יערף in 'יערף כמטר לקחי' as killing, like the עגלה ערופה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And whoever learns Torah not for its own sake, it becomes a poison of death for him. As it says: 'My teaching shall drop (יערף) like rain.' The word עריפה only means killing, as it says: 'And they shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with the bad side: Torah learned with the wrong intentions harms the learner. It proves this from the same פסוק רבא used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יערף can sound like 'drip,' but רבי בנאה connects it to עריפה, the breaking of the neck of the עגלה ערופה. So the same rain-like Torah that gives life to one person 'kills' another. This matches רבא's 'breaks his neck like rain' in Step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: Not for its own sake, with wrong motives
The calf whose neck is broken when a murder victim is found and the killer is unknown

steps.whatToRemember: The same Torah is life for one who learns לשמה and death for one who learns שלא לשמה. This backs up רבא's dew-versus-rain picture.

phrases.english: And anyone who engages in Torah not for its own sake —
it becomes for him a poison of death,
as it says: "My teaching shall drop like the rain,"
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק from Steps 4–7, now read in a darker way.

phrases.english: and 'arifa' means nothing other than killing,
as it says: "And they shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא begun in Step 8 with the negative side.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's reading that Torah 'breaks the neck' of the unworthy
steps.raayaSupportSource: יערף כמטר לקחי, read through the word עריפה in the עגלה ערופה פסוק

steps.title: רבי זירא is too weak to teach halacha, so he is asked for aggada
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא to teach. רבי זירא says he is too weak, so רבי ירמיה asks him for something from אגדה instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said to רבי זירא: Let the master come and teach. He answered: My heart is weak and I am not able. So he said: Let the master tell us a teaching of אגדה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short story that sets up the next teaching. It explains why the next piece is אגדה and not a הלכה lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Teaching הלכה takes hard mental effort, and רבי זירא felt too weak for it. אגדה was seen as lighter, so רבי ירמיה asked for that. This frames the אגדה about the תלמיד חכם that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Let the master come and teach
My heart is weak, I feel faint

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to Rabbi Zeira:
Let the master come and teach.
phrases.notes: He means: teach us a הלכה lesson.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲלַשׁ לִבַּאי וְלָא יָכֵילְנָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: My heart is weak, and I am not able.
Let the master say a teaching of aggada,
phrases.notes: Now רבי ירמיה is speaking again.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A short story that leads into a new אגדה about worthy and unworthy scholars.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative setup: רבי זירא is asked for אגדה because he is too weak for הלכה.

steps.title: How can a person be called a tree of the field?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא quotes רבי יוחנן, who asks about the פסוק 'כי האדם עץ השדה.' Is a person really a tree?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: What does the פסוק 'For man is a tree of the field' mean? Is a person really a tree of the field?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא begins the אגדה by quoting רבי יוחנן's question on a strange-sounding פסוק. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the פסוק seems to say a person is a tree, which makes no sense. The question forces us to find a deeper meaning. The answer will show the פסוק is talking about a תלמיד חכם.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written?
And is it really so? (a question doubting the plain reading)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן —
phrases.english: He said to him: So said Rabbi Yochanan:
What is that which is written: "For man is a tree of the field"?
And is a person a tree of the field?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the אגדה רבי זירא shares in answer to רבי ירמיה's request.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the פסוק mean by comparing a person to a tree of the field?

steps.title: Two verses about trees seem to contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the comparison comes to settle two פסוקים. One says not to cut down the tree, and the other says you may cut it down.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because it is written: 'For from it you may eat, but it you may not cut down.' And it is written: 'It you may destroy and cut down.' How can both be true?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן points to two nearby פסוקים about trees that seem to clash. He sets up the question 'הא כיצד' that the next step will answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One פסוק forbids cutting down a tree. The next פסוק allows it. The phrase 'האדם עץ השדה' hints that both are really about a person, so the contradiction will be solved by talking about two kinds of people.

keyTerms.meaning: You may destroy and cut down
How is this? (how can both פסוקים fit?)

phrases.english: Rather, it is because it is written:
"For from it you may eat, but it you may not cut down,"
and it is written: "It you may destroy and cut down."
How is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering Step 11 by raising a contradiction between two tree פסוקים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים in דברים 20:19–20 about cutting down trees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק forbids cutting the tree and the next one allows it, so they seem to contradict.

steps.title: A worthy scholar is a tree to learn from; an unworthy one is cut down
steps.stepSummary: If the תלמיד חכם is הגון, he is like the fruit tree you eat from and must not cut down. If not, he is like the tree you may cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy תלמיד חכם, then 'from him you may eat, and him you may not cut down.' And if not, then 'him you may destroy and cut down.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן solves the contradiction: the two פסוקים describe two kinds of תלמיד חכם, worthy and unworthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'tree' is the scholar. With a worthy one, you 'eat' from him and must not cut him off. With an unworthy one, the opposite applies. This matches the theme from רבא and רבי בנאה: the worth of the learner decides how Torah plays out.
steps.whatToRemember: The two tree פסוקים are about two kinds of scholars. A worthy תלמיד חכם is a tree you eat from and do not cut down. An unworthy one may be 'cut down.'

phrases.english: If he is a worthy Torah scholar —
"from him you may eat, and him you may not cut down,"
phrases.notes: Now the 'tree' in the פסוק is the scholar himself.

phrases.english: and if not —
"him you may destroy and cut down."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'הא כיצד' of Step 12 and so explains Step 11's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each פסוק refers to a different kind of person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים seem to give opposite rules for the same tree.
steps.terutzMaskana: One פסוק is about a worthy תלמיד חכם and the other about an unworthy one.

steps.title: Iron sharpens iron: scholars sharpen each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא explains the פסוק 'ברזל בברזל יחד': just as one piece of iron sharpens another, two תלמידי חכמים sharpen each other in הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא son of רבי חנינא said: What does the פסוק 'Iron sharpens iron' mean? It teaches you: just as one piece of iron sharpens the other, so too two Torah scholars sharpen each other in הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about Torah study. It compares learning with a partner to two pieces of iron rubbing against each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Iron gets sharp by rubbing against other iron. In the same way, scholars become sharper when they learn together, question each other, and test each other's ideas in הלכה. This adds a new point: learning with others improves understanding.

keyTerms.meaning: To tell you (introducing the lesson of a פסוק)
Just as ... so too (a comparison formula)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a key source for learning בחברותא: two learners pushing each other leads to clearer understanding of הלכה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said:
What is that which is written: "Iron sharpens iron"?
To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה בַּרְזֶל זֶה — אֶחָד מְחַדֵּד אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ,
phrases.english: just as with this iron, one sharpens the other,
so too two Torah scholars —
sharpen one another in halacha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא, מַאי דִּכְתִיב: ״בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יָחַד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new series of teachings about Torah study, following the theme of the תלמיד חכם.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two תלמידי חכמים sharpen each other in הלכה, just as iron sharpens iron.

steps.title: Torah is like fire: it does not burn alone
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה teaches that Torah is compared to fire because fire does not burn from one piece alone. In the same way, Torah does not last with a person who learns alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: Why is Torah compared to fire, as it says, 'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳'? To teach you: just as fire does not burn alone, Torah does not last with someone who learns alone.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה gives a new teaching, comparing Torah to fire. It continues the theme of step 14, that learning together is what makes Torah work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק only says Torah is 'like fire,' so רבה בר בר חנה asks what the comparison teaches. His answer: fire needs more than one piece of wood to keep burning. So Torah needs more than one learner to really stay with a person.

keyTerms.meaning: To tell you, to teach you

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole section: learning Torah with a חברותא is not just nice, it is how Torah stays with you.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said:
Why are words of Torah compared to fire,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הֲלֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ נְאֻם ה׳״,
phrases.english: as it says: "Is not My word like fire, says ה׳"?
To tell you:
just as fire does not burn alone,

phrases.aramaic: אַף דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֵין מִתְקַיְּימִין בִּיחִידִי.
phrases.english: so too, words of Torah do not last with one who is alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another פסוק-based picture to the idea from step 14 that scholars sharpen each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah, like fire, does not last with someone learning alone.

steps.title: A warning to scholars who learn alone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רבה בר בר חנה with a teaching of רבי יוסי בר חנינא. He reads a פסוק as a 'sword' upon scholars who learn alone, and adds that they become foolish.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: What does the פסוק 'A sword upon the בדים, and they shall become foolish' mean? A sword upon the 'enemies' of תלמידי חכמים who learn Torah each alone. And not only that, they become foolish, as it says 'and they shall become foolish.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'this is what' רבי יוסי בר חנינא meant, bringing his teaching as support for the idea that learning alone does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי בר חנינא reads the word בדים as בד בבד, meaning 'each one alone.' So the פסוק becomes a warning to people who learn Torah by themselves. The end of the פסוק, ונאלו, adds that learning alone even makes them foolish.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what [so-and-so] said; this matches his teaching
What is meant by what is written
'Enemies of the scholars,' a polite way to mean the scholars themselves

steps.confusionAlert: The 'enemies of תלמידי חכמים' are not really their enemies. The גמרא avoids saying something harsh directly about scholars, so it says 'their enemies' but means the scholars themselves.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
What is meant by what is written: "A sword upon the baddim, and they shall become foolish"?
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 50:36. He is about to read בדים as 'those who are alone.'

phrases.aramaic: חֶרֶב עַל שׂוֹנְאֵיהֶן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
phrases.english: A sword upon the 'enemies' of Torah scholars
phrases.notes: A polite way of saying the scholars themselves.

phrases.english: who learn Torah each one by himself.
And not only that, but they become foolish,
as it says: "and they shall become foolish."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a matching teaching that supports רבה בר בר חנה's point about learning alone.
steps.raayaObject: The idea from step 15 that Torah does not last with one who learns alone.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוסי בר חנינא's reading of ירמיהו 50:36, 'חרב אל הבדים ונאלו.'

steps.title: Learning alone can even lead to sin
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא goes further: those who learn alone even come to sin. He shows this by matching the word ונאלו to a פסוק where 'acting foolishly' sits right next to 'sinning.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, they sin. Here it is written 'and they shall become foolish,' and there it is written 'for we have acted foolishly and for we have sinned.'
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching continues one step further, saying that learning alone leads not only to foolishness but even to sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is a word match. The same root, נואל, appears in a פסוק in במדבר together with 'we have sinned.' So the 'foolishness' in our פסוק is the kind that brings a person to sin.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even more
It is written here... and it is written there: matching the same word in two פסוקים

phrases.english: And not only that, but they sin.
It is written here: "and they shall become foolish,"
and it is written there:
"for we have acted foolishly and for we have sinned."
phrases.notes: במדבר 12:11. The same word for 'foolish' sits right next to 'sinned.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 16, going from 'they become foolish' to 'they even sin.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learning Torah alone can lead not only to foolishness but to sin, shown by matching the word נואל.

steps.title: A second source linking foolishness and leading astray
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another פסוק to show that this 'foolishness' leads to going wrong: the foolish princes of Zoan led Egypt astray.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, learn it from here: 'The princes of Zoan have become foolish... they have led Egypt astray.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different source for the same point, that the word נואלו connects to going wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the same word, נואלו, is used about leaders whose foolishness caused a whole nation to go astray. This is another way to show that this kind of foolishness ends in wrongdoing.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say; introduces another way or another source

phrases.english: And if you want, say it is learned from here:
"The princes of Zoan have become foolish, and so on,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 19:13. וגו׳ means the פסוק keeps going; the word in square brackets is added by the corrected wording.

phrases.english: they have led Egypt astray."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second source for the same point made in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That the 'foolishness' of נואלו leads to wrongdoing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו 19:13, where foolish princes led Egypt astray.

steps.title: Torah is like wood: small sticks light big ones
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק teaches that Torah is compared to a tree, or wood, because a small stick can light a big one. In the same way, younger students sharpen great scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Why is Torah compared to a tree, as it says, 'It is a tree of life to those who hold on to it'? To teach you: just as a small piece of wood lights a big one, so younger scholars sharpen the great ones.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching with a new picture. Torah is compared to wood, and the lesson is about younger students helping bigger scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 taught that you need a partner. This step adds who can help: even someone smaller than you. A small stick catches fire first and then lights the big log, so a student's questions can sharpen his teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: Small ones, here meaning younger or lesser scholars

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Why are words of Torah compared to a tree,
as it says: "It is a tree of life to those who hold on to it"?
To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה עֵץ קָטָן מַדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדוֹל,
phrases.english: just as a small piece of wood lights a big one,

phrases.aramaic: אַף תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים קְטַנִּים מְחַדְּדִים אֶת הַגְּדוֹלִים.
phrases.english: so too, small Torah scholars sharpen the great ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'why is Torah compared to' pattern as step 15, with a new picture and a new lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Younger students sharpen great scholars, the way a small stick lights a big log.

steps.title: רבי חנינא learned most from his students
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רב נחמן בר יצחק with רבי חנינא's words: he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and most of all from his students.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רבי חנינא said: I learned much from my teachers, more than that from my friends, and from my students more than from all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the 'small sticks light big ones' idea with a personal statement from רבי חנינא, closing this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא ranks his sources of learning, and students come out on top. This matches step 19 exactly: the 'small' students are the ones who sharpen the 'great' teacher the most.
steps.whatToRemember: Torah is learned best together. Like fire, it needs more than one learner (step 15); learning alone leads to foolishness and even sin (steps 16-18); and like wood, even small students light up great teachers (steps 19-20).

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Chanina said:
I learned much from my teachers,
and from my friends more than from my teachers,
and from my students more than from all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 19 with a matching personal teaching.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's idea that small scholars sharpen great ones.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חנינא's statement that he learned most from his students.

steps.title: Two verses about water seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא points out two פסוקים that seem to contradict: one says bring water to the thirsty, the other says the thirsty must go to the water.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר פפא raised a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'To him who is thirsty bring water.' Another says: 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר פפא sets two פסוקים side by side that seem to say opposite things. He is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water stands for Torah, and the thirsty person stands for the student. One פסוק says the water comes to the thirsty person, meaning the teacher goes to the student. The other says the thirsty person must go to the water, meaning the student must find a teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a contradiction (between two sources)

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa raised a contradiction:
It is written: "To him who is thirsty bring water,"
And it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of the teacher-student relationship from steps 19-20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים about water and the thirsty
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק has the water coming to the thirsty person, the other has the thirsty person going to the water.

steps.title: Worthy student versus unworthy student
steps.stepSummary: The answer: if the תלמיד is worthy, the teacher goes to him; if not, the student must go looking for a teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy student, then 'to him who is thirsty bring water.' If not, then 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר פפא settles the contradiction by saying each פסוק speaks about a different kind of student.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים are true, but about different people. A worthy student deserves to have the teacher come to him. A student who is not worthy has to make the effort and go find Torah himself.

phrases.english: If he is a worthy student —
"to him who is thirsty bring water,"
phrases.notes: Meaning the teacher goes out to him.

phrases.english: and if not —
"Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each פסוק refers to a different type of student
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים seem to give opposite instructions about who goes to whom.
steps.terutzMaskana: A worthy student is sought out by the teacher; an unworthy one must seek out the teacher himself.

steps.title: Share your springs, or keep them to yourself?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר חמא points out two back-to-back פסוקים: one says let your springs spread outside, the next says keep them for yourself alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר חמא raised a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'Let your springs be spread outside.' The next says: 'Let them be yours alone.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second contradiction, very similar to the first, is set up. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'springs' are the teacher's Torah. One פסוק says to share it widely, and the very next one says to keep it to yourself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama raised a contradiction:
It is written: "Let your springs be spread outside,"
And it is written: "Let them be yours alone."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel contradiction to step 21, by a different אמורא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says to share the springs outward, the next says to keep them private.

steps.title: Teach the worthy, hold back from the unworthy
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: if the תלמיד is worthy, share your Torah with him; if not, keep it to yourself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a worthy student, 'let your springs be spread outside.' If not, 'let them be yours alone.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר חמא settles his contradiction the same way as before: it depends on whether the student is worthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the focus is on the teacher's choice. With a worthy student, the teacher should pour out his Torah. With an unworthy one, he should hold it back.
steps.whatToRemember: Both contradictions (steps 21-24) are solved the same way: how Torah is passed on depends on whether the student is worthy.

phrases.english: If he is a worthy student —
"Let your springs be spread outside,"
and if not —
"Let them be yours alone."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: worthy versus unworthy student
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים seem to say both to share and to keep the Torah private.
steps.terutzMaskana: Share Torah with a worthy student; keep it from an unworthy one.

steps.title: Torah is like water: it flows to the humble
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר אידי explains that Torah is compared to water because water leaves high places and flows down, and Torah stays only with a humble person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר אידי said: Why is Torah compared to water, as it says 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water'? To teach you: just as water leaves a high place and goes to a low place, so Torah lasts only with someone whose mind is humble.
steps.whatsHappening: Still using the water פסוק, רבי חנינא בר אידי gives a new lesson: why Torah is compared to water at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water never stays on a hilltop; it runs down to the lowest spot. In the same way, Torah does not stay with a proud person who 'raises himself up.' It settles in someone who makes himself low, meaning humble.

keyTerms.meaning: His mind is lowly, he is humble

phrases.english: And Rabbi Ḥanina bar Idi said:
Why are words of Torah compared to water,
as it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water"?
To tell you:
Just as water leaves a high place
and goes to a low place,
so too, words of Torah do not last
except with one whose mind is humble.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אִידִי לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same water פסוק from step 21 to teach a new lesson about humility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah stays only with a humble person, just as water flows only to low places.

steps.title: Torah is like water, wine and milk: kept in simple containers
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא explains that Torah is compared to water, wine and milk because these drinks keep well only in the simplest containers, and Torah stays only with a humble person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אושעיא said: Why is Torah compared to these three drinks, water, wine and milk? As it says 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water,' and 'come, buy and eat... buy wine and milk without money and without price.' To teach you: just as these three drinks keep only in the plainest of containers, so Torah lasts only with someone whose mind is humble.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אושעיא adds a second picture that teaches the same lesson of humility, using all three drinks named in the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא בר אידי used only water and the idea of flowing downward. רבי אושעיא adds wine and milk and uses a new image: these drinks keep best in plain, simple containers, not fancy ones. A person who sees himself as simple and humble is the right 'container' for Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: The plainest, least valuable of containers

steps.whatToRemember: Two images, one lesson: Torah flows down like water and keeps in simple containers like water, wine and milk. Only a humble person holds on to Torah.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Oshaya said:
Why are words of Torah compared
to these three drinks:
to water, to wine, and to milk?
As it is written: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water,"
and it is written: "Come, buy and eat,
and come, buy without money
and without price, wine and milk."
phrases.notes: This is the rest of the same פסוק, ישעיהו 55:1.

phrases.english: To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׁלֹשָׁה מַשְׁקִין הַלָּלוּ אֵין מִתְקַיְּימִין
phrases.english: Just as these three drinks do not keep
except in the plainest of containers —
so too, words of Torah do not last
except with one whose mind is humble.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִשְׁלֹשָׁה מַשְׁקִין הַלָּלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 25 with a broader comparison (three drinks) and a new image (simple containers), reaching the same lesson of humility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah lasts only with a humble person, just as water, wine and milk keep only in the plainest containers.

steps.title: The emperor's daughter mocks רבי יהושע בן חנניה, and he answers with a question about wine
steps.stepSummary: The emperor's daughter says great wisdom is wasted in an ugly body. רבי יהושע בן חנניה asks why her father keeps his wine in clay jars and tells her that important people should use gold and silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what the emperor's daughter said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: 'What a shame, such beautiful wisdom in such an ugly container!' He said to her: 'Does your father keep his wine in clay jars?' She said: 'Then what should we keep it in?' He said: 'You are such important people. Put it in gold and silver vessels!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story to show רבי אושעיא's point from the last step: wine, like Torah, keeps best in a plain container. This step sets up the story, and the result comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The daughter thinks great wisdom should live in a beautiful body. רבי יהושע בן חנניה does not argue back directly. He sets her up to find out for herself what happens when wine goes into fancy vessels.

keyTerms.meaning: An ugly vessel (here meaning an ugly-looking person)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהושע בן חנניה is not really telling her to use gold vessels because they are better. He is setting her up so she will see that wine spoils in them.

phrases.english: As the emperor's daughter said to
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya:
Woe, glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel!
phrases.notes: She is mocking his looks. He was a great scholar but not handsome.

phrases.english: He said to her: Does your father put wine
in clay vessels?
She said to him: Then in what should we put it?
He said to her: You, who are so important,
put it in vessels of gold and silver.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדַאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ בְּרַתֵּיה דְּקֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story to illustrate רבי אושעיא's statement that wine and Torah keep best in simple containers.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אושעיא's teaching that Torah, like wine, stays only in a humble, simple 'vessel'
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי יהושע בן חנניה and the emperor's daughter

steps.title: The wine spoils in the gold vessels, and רבי יהושע בן חנניה explains his lesson
steps.stepSummary: The emperor moves his wine into gold and silver vessels, and it goes sour. He calls in רבי יהושע בן חנניה, who explains that he answered the daughter the same way she spoke to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: She went and told her father. He put the wine in gold and silver vessels, and it turned sour. His servants came and told him. He asked his daughter: 'Who told you to do this?' She said: 'רבי יהושע בן חנניה.' They called him in. The emperor asked: 'Why did you tell her that?' He answered: 'The way she spoke to me, that is how I spoke to her.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its point. The wine spoils in the fancy vessels, and רבי יהושע בן חנניה explains why he gave her that advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sour wine proves the lesson. Something precious keeps best in a plain container, not a fancy one. He was answering her insult: his wisdom keeps well precisely because it sits in a plain 'vessel'.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as, in the same way that

phrases.english: She went and told her father
He put the wine
in vessels of gold and silver, and it turned sour.
They came and told him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ לִבְרַתֵּיהּ: מַאן אֲמַר לָךְ הָכִי?
phrases.english: He said to his daughter: Who told you this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה.
phrases.english: She said to him: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya.

phrases.aramaic: קַרְיוּהוּ. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי אֲמַרְתְּ לַהּ הָכִי?
phrases.english: They called him in. He said to him: Why did you tell her this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי הֵיכִי דַּאֲמַרָה לִי, אֲמַרִי לַהּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: Just as she said to me, so I said to her.
phrases.notes: He means: she mocked my plain 'vessel', so I showed her that fine things keep best in plain vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in step 27 and shows its result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Precious things, like wine and Torah wisdom, keep best in plain, humble vessels, not fancy ones.
steps.whatToRemember: The sour wine in the gold vessels is the whole point of the story. Torah stays best with a humble, plain person, just as wine keeps best in a simple jar.

steps.title: The emperor objects that some good-looking people are learned
steps.stepSummary: The emperor challenges the lesson: there are handsome people who are also learned.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are good-looking people who are learned!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor pushes back on רבי יהושע בן חנניה's lesson. The answer comes in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If wisdom only keeps in a plain 'vessel', handsome people should not be able to hold on to their learning. Yet we see handsome people who are learned, so the lesson seems to fail.

phrases.english: But there are handsome people who are learned!
phrases.notes: The emperor is the one saying this to רבי יהושע בן חנניה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the lesson that רבי יהושע בן חנניה just explained.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that wisdom keeps only in a plain, unattractive 'vessel'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: We can see handsome people who are learned, so good looks do not seem to stop someone from holding on to wisdom.
